title: ICSE CLASS 11 — English | Sentence Types
description: Subject-wise test on Sentence Types (English) for ICSE CLASS 11. 25Q.
subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Identify the type of sentence based on its function: 'How beautifully she sings!'

options.text: Declarative
options.explanation: Declarative sentences are statements and do not express strong emotion.

options.text: Interrogative
options.explanation: Interrogative sentences are questions and do not express strong emotion.

options.text: Imperative
options.explanation: Imperative sentences give commands or requests and do not express strong emotion.

options.text: Exclamatory
options.explanation: Exclamatory sentences express strong emotion or surprise and usually end with an exclamation mark.

questions.explanation: An exclamatory sentence expresses strong emotion or surprise and usually ends with an exclamation mark.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Which of the following is a simple sentence?

options.text: He went to the market, and he bought some vegetables.
options.explanation: This is a compound sentence because it contains two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction.

options.text: Although it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.
options.explanation: This is a complex sentence because it contains an independent clause and a dependent clause.

options.text: The old man walked slowly down the dusty road.
options.explanation: This sentence has one subject and one finite verb, making it a simple sentence.

options.text: She studied hard so that she could pass the exam.
options.explanation: This is a complex sentence because it contains an independent clause and a dependent clause.

questions.explanation: A simple sentence contains only one independent clause and expresses a single complete thought.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Choose the option that correctly identifies the sentence type: 'He is intelligent, but he lacks confidence.'

options.text: Simple Sentence
options.explanation: A simple sentence contains only one independent clause.

options.text: Compound Sentence
options.explanation: This sentence contains two independent clauses joined by 'but', making it a compound sentence.

options.text: Complex Sentence
options.explanation: A complex sentence contains an independent clause and a dependent clause.

options.text: Exclamatory Sentence
options.explanation: An exclamatory sentence expresses strong emotion or surprise and usually ends with an exclamation mark.

questions.explanation: A compound sentence consists of two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is an imperative sentence?

options.text: What a wonderful surprise it was!

options.text: Did you complete your homework on time?
options.explanation: This is an interrogative sentence because it is a question.

options.text: Please submit your assignments by Friday.
options.explanation: This sentence is an imperative sentence because it gives a polite request or instruction.

options.text: The sun rises in the east.
options.explanation: This is a declarative sentence because it states a fact.

questions.explanation: An imperative sentence expresses a command, request, or instruction.

questions.question: Identify the complex sentence among the given options.

options.text: The dog barked loudly, and the cat ran away.
options.explanation: This is a compound sentence because it contains two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction.

options.text: Since you are busy, I will come later.
options.explanation: This sentence contains an independent clause and a dependent clause, making it a complex sentence.

options.text: Open the window immediately.
options.explanation: This is an imperative sentence because it gives a command or instruction.

options.text: We enjoyed the picnic in the park.
options.explanation: This is a simple sentence because it contains only one independent clause.

questions.explanation: A complex sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

questions.question: Transform the following simple sentence into a complex sentence while retaining its meaning: 'Despite his hard work, he failed the exam.'

options.text: He worked hard, but he failed the exam.
options.explanation: This sentence does not convey the same contrast as the original sentence.

options.text: He worked hard and failed the exam.
options.explanation: This sentence does not convey the same contrast as the original sentence.

options.text: Although he worked hard, he failed the exam.
options.explanation: This sentence uses a subordinating conjunction to introduce a dependent clause, maintaining the original meaning of contrast.

options.text: He failed the exam because he did not work hard.
options.explanation: This sentence changes the original meaning by implying a cause-and-effect relationship.

questions.explanation: The original sentence implies a contrast, and the transformation should maintain this meaning.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Transform the following compound sentence into a simple sentence: 'She finished her work, and then she went home.'

options.text: She finished her work because she wanted to go home.
options.explanation: This sentence changes the original meaning by implying a cause-and-effect relationship.

options.text: After she finished her work, she went home.
options.explanation: This sentence is a complex sentence because it contains an independent clause and a dependent clause.

options.text: Having finished her work, she went home.
options.explanation: This sentence uses a participial phrase to reduce the two independent clauses into a single simple sentence, conveying the sequence of actions.

options.text: She went home, for she had finished her work.
options.explanation: This sentence is a complex sentence because it contains an independent clause and a dependent clause.

questions.explanation: The transformation should result in a sentence that conveys the same meaning but with only one independent clause.

questions.question: **Assertion (A):** The sentence 'Go home now' is an imperative sentence. **Reason (R):** Imperative sentences always end with an exclamation mark.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Reason R is false because imperative sentences do not always end with an exclamation mark.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
options.explanation: Reason R is false because imperative sentences do not always end with an exclamation mark.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.
options.explanation: Assertion A is true because 'Go home now' is indeed an imperative sentence, but Reason R is false because imperative sentences do not always end with an exclamation mark.

options.text: A is false, but R is true.
options.explanation: Assertion A is true, and Reason R is false.

questions.explanation: Imperative sentences can end with either a full stop or an exclamation mark, depending on the intensity of the command or request.

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is a compound-complex sentence?

options.text: The rain poured down, but we continued our journey.
options.explanation: This is a compound sentence because it contains two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction, but it lacks a dependent clause.

options.text: Because it was raining, we stayed indoors.
options.explanation: This is a complex sentence because it contains an independent clause and a dependent clause, but it lacks another independent clause.

options.text: Although it was late, he continued to study, and his brother slept soundly.
options.explanation: This sentence contains two independent clauses ('he continued to study' and 'his brother slept soundly') and a dependent clause ('Although it was late'), making it a compound-complex sentence.

options.text: He went to the library to borrow a book.
options.explanation: This is a simple sentence because it contains only one independent clause.

questions.explanation: A compound-complex sentence contains two or more independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Consider the sentence: 'He bought the book which was recommended by his teacher.' Which of the following statements is true about this sentence?

options.text: It is a compound sentence with two independent clauses.
options.explanation: The sentence does not contain two independent clauses.

options.text: It is a simple sentence as it has only one subject-verb pair.
options.explanation: The sentence contains a dependent clause, making it not a simple sentence.

options.text: It is a complex sentence containing an adjective clause.
options.explanation: The sentence contains one independent clause ('He bought the book') and a dependent adjective clause ('which was recommended by his teacher'), making it a complex sentence.

options.text: It is a complex sentence containing an adverbial clause of reason.
options.explanation: The dependent clause in the sentence functions as an adjective clause, not an adverbial clause of reason.

questions.explanation: The sentence contains one independent clause and a dependent clause that functions as an adjective clause.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Identify the simple sentence among the following options.

options.text: Although it was raining, we went for a walk.
options.explanation: This sentence contains a dependent clause ('Although it was raining') and an independent clause ('we went for a walk'), making it a complex sentence.

options.text: We went for a walk, and we enjoyed the fresh air.
options.explanation: This sentence contains two independent clauses joined by the conjunction 'and', making it a compound sentence.

options.text: We went for a walk in the rain.
options.explanation: This sentence has one subject ('we') and one predicate ('went for a walk in the rain') and expresses a complete thought without any conjunctions joining multiple clauses, making it a simple sentence.

options.text: We went for a walk because it was raining.
options.explanation: This sentence contains an independent clause ('We went for a walk') and a dependent clause ('because it was raining'), making it a complex sentence.

questions.explanation: A simple sentence has only one independent clause and no dependent clauses. Option C contains one subject ('we') and one predicate ('went for a walk in the rain') and expresses a complete thought without any conjunctions joining multiple clauses.
questions.hint: A simple sentence does not contain any dependent clauses or multiple independent clauses joined by conjunctions.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is a declarative sentence?

options.text: What a beautiful day it is!
options.explanation: This is an exclamatory sentence, which expresses strong emotion and ends with an exclamation mark.

options.text: Please close the door.
options.explanation: This is an imperative sentence, which gives a command or makes a request.

options.text: Do you know the answer?
options.explanation: This is an interrogative sentence, which asks a question and ends with a question mark.

options.text: The sun rises in the east.
options.explanation: This is a declarative sentence as it makes a statement and ends with a period.

questions.explanation: A declarative sentence makes a statement or expresses a fact or opinion and usually ends with a period. Options A, B, and C are exclamatory, imperative, and interrogative sentences, respectively.
questions.hint: A declarative sentence ends with a period and makes a statement.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Convert the following simple sentence into a compound sentence: 'Despite his hard work, he failed.'

options.text: He failed because he did not work hard.
options.explanation: This sentence changes the meaning of the original sentence by introducing a cause-effect relationship.

options.text: Although he worked hard, he failed.
options.explanation: This sentence is a complex sentence, not a compound sentence, as it contains a dependent clause ('Although he worked hard').

options.text: He worked hard, yet he failed.
options.explanation: This sentence joins two independent clauses ('He worked hard' and 'he failed') with the coordinating conjunction 'yet,' making it a compound sentence that retains the original meaning.

options.text: He worked hard, and he failed.
options.explanation: While this is a compound sentence, it does not convey the contrast implied by 'despite' in the original sentence.

questions.explanation: A compound sentence consists of two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction. Option C uses 'yet' to join two independent clauses ('He worked hard' and 'he failed'), expressing a contrast, which is appropriate for the original meaning of 'despite.'
questions.hint: A compound sentence requires two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction like 'and,' 'but,' 'or,' etc.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: In the sentence, 'She is intelligent, but she is also very lazy,' what type of conjunction is 'but'?

options.text: Subordinating conjunction
options.explanation: Subordinating conjunctions introduce dependent clauses (e.g., 'although,' 'because').

options.text: Correlative conjunction
options.explanation: Correlative conjunctions come in pairs (e.g., 'either...or,' 'neither...nor').

options.text: Coordinating conjunction
options.explanation: 'But' is a coordinating conjunction as it joins two independent clauses ('She is intelligent' and 'she is also very lazy').

options.text: Adverbial conjunction
options.explanation: Adverbial conjunctions (e.g., 'however,' 'therefore') are used to connect ideas but are not classified as coordinating conjunctions.

questions.explanation: 'But' is one of the FANBOYS (For, And, Nor, But, Or, Yet, So), which are used to join two independent clauses of equal grammatical rank, forming a compound sentence.
questions.hint: Conjunctions that join two independent clauses of equal rank are called coordinating conjunctions.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Transform the complex sentence into a simple sentence: 'As soon as the bell rang, the students rushed out.'

options.text: The bell rang, and the students rushed out.
options.explanation: This is a compound sentence with two independent clauses joined by 'and.'

options.text: The students rushed out when the bell rang.
options.explanation: This is a complex sentence as it contains a dependent clause ('when the bell rang').

options.text: On the ringing of the bell, the students rushed out.
options.explanation: This sentence uses a participial phrase ('On the ringing of the bell') to modify the main clause ('the students rushed out'), resulting in a single independent clause.

options.text: The students rushed out because the bell rang.
options.explanation: This is a complex sentence as it contains a dependent clause ('because the bell rang').

questions.explanation: A simple sentence must contain only one independent clause. Option C rephrases the action of the bell ringing into a participial phrase ('On the ringing of the bell') that modifies the main clause ('the students rushed out'), thus creating a single independent clause.
questions.hint: A simple sentence has only one independent clause. Try to reduce the sentence to a single clause by rephrasing dependent elements.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Identify the type of sentence: 'Although she was tired, she continued to work, and she finished the project on time.'

options.text: Simple sentence
options.explanation: A simple sentence has only one independent clause and no dependent clauses.

options.text: Compound sentence
options.explanation: A compound sentence has two or more independent clauses but no dependent clauses.

options.text: Complex sentence
options.explanation: A complex sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

options.text: Compound-complex sentence
options.explanation: This sentence has one dependent clause ('Although she was tired') and two independent clauses ('she continued to work' and 'she finished the project on time'), making it a compound-complex sentence.

questions.explanation: This sentence has one dependent clause ('Although she was tired') and two independent clauses ('she continued to work' and 'she finished the project on time') joined by the coordinating conjunction 'and'. Therefore, it is a compound-complex sentence.
questions.hint: A compound-complex sentence contains at least one dependent clause and two or more independent clauses.
questions.subject: icse11-english

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

options.text: A is true, but R is false.

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is a **Simple Sentence**?

options.text: She went to the market and bought some fruits.
options.explanation: This sentence has two independent clauses joined by 'and', making it a Compound Sentence.

options.text: She went to the market to buy some fruits.
options.explanation: This sentence has a single subject ('She') and a single verb phrase ('went to the market to buy some fruits'), making it a Simple Sentence.

options.text: She went to the market because she wanted to buy some fruits.
options.explanation: This sentence has a dependent clause ('because she wanted to buy some fruits'), making it a Complex Sentence.

options.text: If she went to the market, she would buy some fruits.
options.explanation: This sentence has a dependent clause ('If she went to the market') and an independent clause, making it a Complex Sentence.

questions.explanation: A Simple Sentence has only one independent clause with a subject and a predicate. Option B is correct because it contains a single subject ('She') and a single verb phrase ('went to the market to buy some fruits') without any dependent clauses.
questions.hint: Look for a sentence with only one subject and one verb phrase, without any conjunctions or dependent clauses.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Identify the type of the following sentence: **'Although he was tired, he completed his homework.'**

options.text: Simple Sentence
options.explanation: A Simple Sentence has only one independent clause with no dependent clauses.

options.text: Complex Sentence
options.explanation: This sentence has one independent clause ('he completed his homework') and one dependent clause ('Although he was tired').

options.text: Compound Sentence
options.explanation: A Compound Sentence has two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (e.g., and, but, or).

options.text: Compound-Complex Sentence
options.explanation: A Compound-Complex Sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.

questions.explanation: A Complex Sentence contains one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. Here, 'he completed his homework' is the independent clause, and 'Although he was tired' is the dependent clause introduced by the subordinating conjunction 'Although.'

questions.question: Choose the correct transformation of the following sentence into a **Negative Sentence**: **'He is a very talented musician.'**

options.text: He is not a very talented musician.
options.explanation: This is a correct transformation, but it does not emphasize the negation as strongly as Option B.

options.text: He is not a very talented musician at all.
options.explanation: This is the most grammatically correct and natural transformation, emphasizing the negation.

options.text: He is not a talented musician.
options.explanation: This transformation changes the meaning slightly by omitting 'very'.

options.text: He is never a talented musician.
options.explanation: This transformation changes the meaning by using 'never' instead of 'not'.

questions.explanation: To transform a sentence into a Negative Sentence, we add 'not' after the auxiliary verb ('is') and retain the rest of the structure. Option B is the most grammatically correct and natural transformation, emphasizing the negation.
questions.hint: Add 'not' after the auxiliary verb ('is') and ensure the sentence remains grammatically correct.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is an example of a **Compound Sentence**?

options.text: Unless you study hard, you will fail.
options.explanation: This is a Complex Sentence because it has a dependent clause ('Unless you study hard') and an independent clause.

options.text: I wanted to go to the party, but I had to finish my project.
options.explanation: This is a Compound Sentence because it has two independent clauses joined by the conjunction 'but'.

options.text: The man who came here yesterday is my uncle.
options.explanation: This is a Complex Sentence because it has a dependent clause ('who came here yesterday').

options.text: Running fast, he reached the station on time.
options.explanation: This is a Simple Sentence with a participial phrase ('Running fast').

questions.explanation: A Compound Sentence consists of two or more independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so). Option B is correct because it has two independent clauses ('I wanted to go to the party' and 'I had to finish my project') joined by the conjunction 'but.'
questions.hint: Look for a sentence with two independent clauses joined by a coordinating conjunction (e.g., and, but, or).
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question:
**Case-Based Question:**
Read the following passage and answer the question below:
'The weather was extremely hot. The children decided to go for a swim. They went to the nearby lake and enjoyed themselves thoroughly.'
Which of the following sentences correctly combines the above sentences into a **Complex Sentence**?

options.text: The weather was extremely hot, so the children decided to go for a swim.
options.explanation: This is a Compound Sentence because it has two independent clauses joined by 'so'.

options.text: The children decided to go for a swim, and they went to the lake.
options.explanation: This is a Compound Sentence because it has two independent clauses joined by 'and'.

options.text: Because the weather was extremely hot, the children decided to go for a swim and went to the nearby lake.
options.explanation: This is a Complex Sentence because it has a dependent clause ('Because the weather was extremely hot') and an independent clause ('the children decided to go for a swim and went to the nearby lake').

options.text: The children went to the lake because the weather was hot and they decided to go for a swim.
options.explanation: This sentence is grammatically incorrect as it combines two independent clauses with 'because' without proper structure.

questions.explanation: A Complex Sentence must have one independent clause and at least one dependent clause. Option C is correct because it uses the subordinating conjunction 'Because' to introduce the dependent clause ('Because the weather was extremely hot'), followed by the independent clause ('the children decided to go for a swim and went to the nearby lake').
questions.hint: Look for a sentence that uses a subordinating conjunction (e.g., because, although, if) to introduce a dependent clause.
questions.subject: icse11-english

questions.question: Identify the type of the following sentence: **'He not only completed his assignment but also helped his friend.'**

options.text: Simple Sentence
options.explanation: A Simple Sentence has only one independent clause with no dependent clauses.

options.text: Complex Sentence
options.explanation: A Complex Sentence has one independent clause and at least one dependent clause.

options.text: Compound Sentence
options.explanation: This sentence has two independent clauses joined by the correlative conjunction 'not only...but also'.

options.text: Compound-Complex Sentence
options.explanation: A Compound-Complex Sentence has at least two independent clauses and at least one dependent clause.

questions.explanation: The sentence is a Compound Sentence because it consists of two independent clauses ('He completed his assignment' and 'He helped his friend') joined by the correlative conjunction 'not only...but also.' The structure does not include any dependent clauses.
questions.hint: Look for a sentence with two independent clauses joined by a correlative conjunction (e.g., not only...but also, either...or).
questions.subject: icse11-english
